                                        variations of 3D scene benchmarks, according to the parameterized constraints of compositional, relational and observational scene com-
                                        plexities, to meet different benchmarking needs of analyzing the VLM’s successes and failures in spatial reasoning tasks.

                                                                  2
                                                                    2.2. Layout Generation in 3D Scene Generation
                                                                    The main focus of InfiniBench design is the creation of
                                                                    scene layout, which defines the placement, orientation, and
                                                                    relationships of objects in the scene. One can leverage the
                                                                    reasoning capabilities of LLMs to directly produce a lay-
                                                                    out and then instruct a 3D engine to place assets in the
                                                                    scene [7, 44, 46, 67]. To improve the coherence of gener-
                                                                    ated layouts, some works guide LLMs with structural tem-
                                                                    plates [22] or represent scenes as graphs to facilitate com-
                                                                    positional generation [8, 19, 23]. However, the generated
 Unrealistic object   Out-of-boundary       Overlapped              scene’s complexity is constrained by current LLMs’ flawed
   orientations           objects            objects                spatial logic. As shown in Figure 2, as the number of ob-
                                                                    jects and the intricacy of constraints increase, these methods
     Figure 2. Limitations of LLM-based layout generation           frequently produce physically implausible layouts, such as
                                                                    those with unrealistic object orientations, out-of-boundary
                                                                    objects or overlapped objects.
structed view after passing an occlusion check. A navigable            To address this challenge and ensure the scalability of
path is then planned to link these viewpoints.                      generating complex scenes, we proposed a more robust ap-
   We validate the efficacy of InfiniBench by generating            proach that separates high-level planning from low-level ex-
scenes with different scene complexities and comparing the          ecution. Instead of tasking the LLM to generate the ex-
generated scenes with procedural and LLM-based genera-              act scene layout, we use LLM to generate high-level con-
tion methods. Results showed that InfiniBench simultane-            straints about object arrangement. These constraints are
ously ensures prompt fidelity and physical plausibility, and        then fed into a dedicated optimizer that generates a phys-
successfully generates complex and high-density 3D scenes           ically coherent 3D scene. By using optimization-based pro-
required by user prompts, where other methods fail.                 cedural generation frameworks [18, 43] that are effective in
    We further showed that customizable benchmarks gen-             3D scene synthesis [63, 64, 68], we designed an improved
erated by InfiniBench facilitate in-depth analysis of VLM’s         optimizer for generating complex scenes and wrap this op-
failure modes in various spatial reasoning tasks, including         timizer within an LLM-based agentic framework, making
measurement (e.g. metric distance estimation), perspective-         the entire pipeline both powerful and user-friendly.
taking (e.g. object counting) and spatiotemporal tracking
(e.g. identification of order identification) [6]. Such cus-
tomizability in benchmarking would also be a key enabler
of enhancing VLM’s spatial reasoning capabilities, via spa-
tially grounded training or prompt tuning.

As shown in Figure 1, the core of InfiniBench design is a
three-stage pipeline, which consists of (1) an LLM-based
                                                                                                                     3.2. Layout Optimization for Complex Scenes
agentic framework that translates user prompts of scene de-                                                          When the scene complexity grows, hierarchical optimiza-
scriptions into procedural constraints through iterative re-                                                         tion methods used in the existing procedural generation
finement; (2) a cluster-based layout engine that optimizes                                                           frameworks such as Infinigen [43] and ProcTHOR [18]
these constraints into physically plausible 3D scenes; and                                                           would fail, because they first fix the positions of large ob-
(3) a task-aware camera trajectory algorithm that renders                                                            jects (e.g. desks and beds) and usually result in unsolvable
the 3D scene into an informative video as VLM input.                                                                 states where there is no space for smaller objects (e.g. chairs
                                                                                                                     around the desk), as shown in Figure 6(a).

                                                                                           Evaluation Metrics. We focus on two challenging aspects
                                                                                           of scene complexity: the total number of objects and the
                                                                                           scene occupancy ratio. We evaluate the generated scenes
                                                                                           using the following metrics:
                                                                                           • Prompt fidelity, which measures the alignment between
                                                                                             the generated scene and text prompt. It is calculated as
                                                                                             the accuracy of the generated scene’s object count and oc-
                                                                                             cupancy ratio against ground truth values in text prompt.
                                                                                           • Text-image alignment, which measure the semantic align-
                                                                                             ment as the CLIP score [42] between the text prompt and
                                                                                             the rendered top-down image of generated scene.
Figure 8. An example of optimized camera trajectory and the cor-
responding video frames
                                                                                           • Layout realism, scored by a GPT-5 evaluator as suggested
                                                                                             by Scenethesis [36], incorporating key factors such as
generate physically plausible 3D scenes that are superior to                                 spatial coherence and functional plausibility.
those from existing baseline methods, in terms of correct-                                 • Physical plausibility, measured by the number of phys-
ness and quality? 2) How effective are different components                                  ically impossible artifacts, especially the count of out-
of InfiniBench in such generation?                                                           of-boundary objects (#OB) and pairs of collided objects
                                                                                             (#CN), as suggested by SceneWeaver [60].

C.1. Cluster Definition and Identification                                    produce more realistic renderings of these example scenes.
We define the root of a cluster as an object situated at
the highest level of the hierarchy (typically large furniture,                E. Details of the Camera Trajectory Optimiza-
such as tables or desks). Objects at lower hierarchy levels                       tion Algorithm
are designated as child objects if they maintain a “stable

against” spatial relationship with a parent object. Informa-

tion regarding these clusters is dynamically retrieved and
                                                                              sual coverage of task-related objects, we constrain the op-
updated from the global “scene state” throughout the opti-

mization process.

C.2. Augmented Action Space                                                   restrict the roll angle (θx ) to zero to maintain view stabil-
                                                                              ity. Consequently, the optimization is performed over the
In standard rigid-hierarchy optimization, the action space                    remaining four degrees of freedom: the horizontal position
for individual objects comprises addition, resampling, dele-                  coordinates (x, y) and the rotational angles for yaw (θy ) and
tion, translation, rotation, relation plane changes, relation                 pitch (θz ). This configuration allows the camera to freely
target changes, and swapping. To facilitate cluster-based                     navigate accessible areas on the horizontal plane and adjust
optimization, we augment this space by adding the follow-                     its viewing angle to effectively frame relevant spatial fea-
ing cluster-specific operations:                                              tures.

   child objects.                                                             builds a path to view every task-related object in the scene.

F. Details of InfiniBench Implementation
                                                                                 - Path tracing based               -Rasterization based
As illustrated in Figure 23, we employ the Blender Cycles                        - Time consuming                   - Real-time rendering
engine, which utilizes path tracing, to achieve photoreal-                       - High quality                     - Low quality
istic frame rendering. A critical parameter in this process
is the number of path-tracing samples. While 8192 samples
are typically recommended to produce noise-free images (as              Figure 23. Comparison of image quality across different renderers.
shown in Figure 24), this setting is computationally expen-
sive, requiring approximately 5 minutes per frame. To op-
timize for efficiency without compromising quality, we ad-
